titolo: Enron – The $63 Billion Company Built on Fake Profits
descrizione:
In August 2000, Enron's stock peaked near $90 and the company was valued at about $63 billion. Sixteen months later, it filed for the largest corporate bankruptcy in US history up to that time. How did America's seventh-largest company by revenue disappear so fast?

This investigation follows the rise of Enron, the accounting tricks that hid billions in debt, the partnerships run by its own CFO, and the collapse that ended Arthur Andersen and reshaped corporate law through the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. All facts come from SEC filings, court records and major newspapers.

fatti: In August 2000 Enron's market value peaked at roughly $63 billion, with shares near $90
Fortune named Enron 'America's Most Innovative Company' for six consecutive years, 1996 to 2001
Enron reported $100.8 billion in revenue for 2000
On December 2, 2001 Enron filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, then the largest in US history
Open question: how did a company reporting record profits collapse in months
Enron formed in 1985 from the merger of Houston Natural Gas and InterNorth
Kenneth Lay became chairman and CEO
Deregulation of natural gas and electricity markets in the 1990s let Enron trade energy contracts
Jeffrey Skilling joined in 1990 and pushed Enron to become a trading company
Enron launched EnronOnline in November 1999, an internet trading platform
In 1992 the SEC approved mark-to-market accounting for Enron's gas trading business
Under this method, expected profits from long-term contracts were booked immediately
Estimated future profits were based on Enron's own models
Cash often did not arrive for years, or at all
Skilling became president and COO in 1997 and CEO in February 2001
Andrew Fastow became CFO in 1998
Enron created off-balance-sheet entities, including LJM partnerships launched in 1999
Fastow ran LJM1 and LJM2 while serving as Enron's CFO
Enron sold assets to these entities and moved debt off its books
The Raptor vehicles were backed largely by Enron's own stock
Broadband and international projects such as the Dabhol power plant in India lost money
Skilling resigned as CEO on August 14, 2001 after about six months, citing personal reasons
Sherron Watkins, an Enron vice president, sent Lay a memo in August 2001 warning of accounting problems
Enron stock fell to around $40 by late August 2001
On October 16, 2001 Enron reported a $618 million third-quarter loss
It announced a $1.2 billion reduction in shareholder equity tied to the LJM partnerships
The SEC opened an inquiry in October 2001
On November 8, 2001 Enron restated earnings back to 1997, reducing profits by about $586 million
Fastow was removed as CFO in late October 2001
Dynegy agreed to buy Enron on November 9, 2001, then walked away on November 28
Credit agencies cut Enron's rating to junk on November 28, 2001
Shares fell below $1
Enron filed for Chapter 11 on December 2, 2001 listing roughly $63 billion in assets
Thousands of employees lost jobs, and many lost retirement savings invested in Enron stock
Arthur Andersen was Enron's auditor
Andersen employees shredded Enron-related documents as the SEC inquiry began
In June 2002 Andersen was convicted of obstruction of justice
The Supreme Court overturned the conviction in 2005
By then the firm had lost its clients and most of its roughly 28,000 US employees
Fastow pleaded guilty in January 2004 and was sentenced in 2006 to six years in prison
Skilling was convicted in May 2006 on 19 counts and sentenced to 24 years and 4 months, later reduced to 14 years
Lay was convicted in May 2006 but died in July 2006 before sentencing
Congress passed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in July 2002
The law requires CEOs and CFOs to certify financial statements
Answer: profits were booked from projections and debt was hidden in entities Enron controlled
Reported earnings did not match real cash
The $63 billion valuation rested on numbers few people could verify
Lesson: when a business cannot be explained simply and cash does not match profits, ask why
Ending line: Subscribe for the next one.

_correzioni: Description: 'Sixteen months later' kept (Aug 2000 to Dec 2001 = 16 months); fine, but 'seventh-largest company by revenue' fixed to 'seventh-largest company in the US by revenue' (Fortune 500 ranking for 2000)
Fortune 'Most Innovative' streak: it was six consecutive years 1996-2001, correct; kept
Revenue 2000: $100.8 billion correct; kept
Dynegy/Enron: removed ambiguity; Dynegy agreed Nov 9, 2001 and withdrew Nov 28, 2001

Chapter title 'Sixteen Days to Bankruptcy' changed to 'Three Weeks to Bankruptcy' because Nov 8 to Dec 2 is 24 days and the Dynegy deal/credit cut sequence spans about three weeks; 'Sixteen' was inaccurate
Skilling: joined Enron in 1990 (Enron Finance), correct; 'Skilling resigned August 14, 2001 after about six months' correct
Skilling became president and COO in 1997 (Dec 1996 announced, effective Jan 1997); CEO Feb 2001 correct; kept
Stock 'below $40 by late summer 2001': it was about $36-40 in late August; made safer: 'fell to around $40 by late August 2001'
Enron stock below $1: reached about $0.26 by Nov 30, 2001; kept as 'fell below $1'
Assets at bankruptcy: Enron listed $63.4 billion in assets (correct); kept
Third-quarter loss: $618 million net loss, correct; $1.2 billion equity reduction correct
Restatement Nov 8, 2001: reduced profits by about $586 million since 1997, correct
SEC inquiry: informal inquiry opened Oct 22, 2001; kept as October 2001
Fastow removed Oct 24, 2001, correct
Andersen convicted June 15, 2002; Supreme Court overturned May 31, 2005; kept. Employees: about 28,000 US employees, kept
Fastow pleaded guilty Jan 2004, sentenced Sept 2006 to six years (reduced from 10-year plea deal), correct
Skilling convicted May 25, 2006 on 19 counts, sentenced to 24 years 4 months, later reduced to 14 years (2013), correct
Lay convicted May 2006, died July 5, 2006, correct
Sarbanes-Oxley signed July 30, 2002, correct
Mark-to-market: SEC approved in January 1992 for Enron's gas trading (Skilling-era unit), correct
Enron formed 1985 from Houston Natural Gas and InterNorth, correct; EnronOnline launched Nov 1999, correct; LJM launched 1999 (LJM1 June 1999, LJM2 Oct 1999), correct
Peak stock: $90.75 in Aug 2000 and market cap about $60-70 billion; kept as 'roughly $63 billion' is commonly cited
